input: Learn to brew my own craft beer at home

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Brewing ranges from simple extract kits to all-grain brewing — the starting point completely changes the equipment, steps, and learning curve involved.
Whether this is a solo hobby or a shared activity with friends or family affects batch sizes, social motivations, and how the plan is structured.
The style of beer they want to brew (e.g. IPA, stout, lager, wheat beer) determines ingredients, fermentation conditions, and which recipes to target first.
Startup equipment costs can range from $50 for a basic kit to $500+ for a full all-grain setup — budget determines what is realistically achievable.
Available space (apartment, garage, house) and climate affect which fermentation methods, equipment sizes, and temperature control solutions are practical.
Knowing whether the goal is to produce one drinkable batch, develop an ongoing hobby, or eventually brew competitively shapes how deep and structured the plan needs to be.
Their preferred learning format — books, video tutorials, local homebrew clubs, or kits with instructions — determines what the immediate first action should be.

gold.taskTitle: Learn to brew craft beer at home
gold.taskDescription: The user wants to learn how to brew their own craft beer at home, starting from their current level of experience.

questions.title: What is your current experience level with homebrewing?
questions.description: Understanding whether the user is a complete beginner, has tried a kit once, or has some brewing knowledge determines where the learning plan starts — extract kits, partial mash, or all-grain.

questions.title: What style of beer do you most want to brew first?
questions.description: The target beer style (IPA, stout, lager, wheat, sour, etc.) drives ingredient selection, fermentation temperature needs, and which beginner recipes are most relevant.

questions.title: How much are you willing to spend on startup equipment?
questions.description: Budget is one of the biggest practical constraints — entry-level extract kits start around $50-80, while a full all-grain setup can cost $300-600+. This determines the recommended gear list.

questions.title: Where in your home will you be brewing and fermenting?
questions.description: Available space — kitchen, garage, basement, or apartment — and ambient temperature conditions affect equipment size choices, temperature control methods, and fermentation feasibility.

questions.title: Are you brewing solo or with others regularly?
questions.description: If brewing is a shared activity with a partner, friend, or group, batch size, collaboration tools, and social learning resources (like a club) become more relevant to the plan.

questions.title: What does success look like — one good batch or an ongoing hobby?
questions.description: The user's end goal — producing a single drinkable batch, developing a regular brewing routine, or eventually entering competitions — determines how structured and progressive the plan needs to be.

questions.title: How do you prefer to learn new practical skills?
questions.description: Preferred learning format — step-by-step books, YouTube tutorials, starter kits with guides, or joining a local homebrew club — determines what the very first concrete action should be.
